claim: The brain receives outdated sensory information when interacting with the dynamic world due to the time required for neural transmission and processing.
source: When interacting with the dynamic world, the brain receives outdated sensory information, due to the time required for neural transmission and processing.
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental premise in the abstract and is supported by established scientific understanding of neural processing delays.

claim: During early stimulus-evoked activity, position representations of moving objects were activated substantially earlier than the equivalent activity evoked by unpredictable flashes.
source: During early stimulus-evoked activity, position representations of moving objects were activated substantially earlier than the equivalent activity evoked by unpredictable flashes, aligning the earliest representations of moving stimuli with their real-time positions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the EEG decoding analysis presented in the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The earliest representations of moving stimuli align with their real-time positions.
source: During early stimulus-evoked activity, position representations of moving objects were activated substantially earlier than the equivalent activity evoked by unpredictable flashes, aligning the earliest representations of moving stimuli with their real-time positions.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the data analysis showing near-zero latency for early representations.

claim: The predictability of straight trajectories enables full compensation for neural delays accumulated early in stimulus processing.
source: These findings indicate that the predictability of straight trajectories enables full compensation for the neural delays accumulated early in stimulus processing, but that delays still accumulate across later stages of cortical processing.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental findings showing temporal alignment of early representations with real-time position.

claim: Delays still accumulate across later stages of cortical processing after early compensation.
source: These findings indicate that the predictability of straight trajectories enables full compensation for the neural delays accumulated early in stimulus processing, but that delays still accumulate across later stages of cortical processing.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis showing similar slopes for static and motion regression lines during feedforward processing.

claim: Prediction is considered a core objective of the central nervous system by many researchers.
source: Indeed, many researchers consider prediction to be a core objective of the central nervous system (Friston, 2010; Clark, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work by Friston and Clark.

claim: The brain can compensate for neural transmission delays through prediction using information from the past.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that the brain can compensate for neural transmission delays through prediction: using information from the past to predict what is happening in the present (Nijhawan, 1994; Kiebel et al., 2008; Friston et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on predictive processing.

claim: Retinal ganglion cells extrapolate the represented position of moving stimuli by responding to the leading edge.
source: By responding to the leading edge of moving stimuli, retinal ganglion cells extrapolate the represented position of those stimuli, and are thought to transmit these extrapolated representations to visual cortex, thereby compensating for some of the lag that arises during transmission.
evidence: This is based on neurophysiological recordings cited in the text (Berry et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2013; Johnston and Lagnado, 2015; Liu et al., 2021; Souihel and Cessac, 2021).

claim: Motion extrapolation mechanisms exist as early as the retina.
source: For example, neurophysiological recordings in animals reveal motion extrapolation mechanisms as early as the retina (Berry et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2013; Johnston and Lagnado, 2015; Liu et al., 2021; Souihel and Cessac, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to animal neurophysiology studies.

claim: Pre-cortical extrapolation mechanisms allow primary visual cortex to represent the position of a moving object with reduced latency.
source: These pre-cortical extrapolation mechanisms should effectively allow primary visual cortex to represent the position of a moving object with reduced latency, as observed in both cat and macaque V1 (Jancke et al., 2004; Subramaniyan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in cat and macaque V1.

claim: Position representations in areas V4 and V5 are shifted for moving objects.
source: On the one hand, there is suggestive evidence that position representations in areas V4 (Sundberg et al., 2006) and V5 (Maus et al., 2013a) are shifted for moving objects, potentially reflecting the effect of motion extrapolation in those areas.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies examining V4 and V5.

claim: Twelve observers viewed sequences of black discs that were either flashed in one of 37 possible positions or smoothly moved through positions on a hexagonal grid.
source: Twelve observers viewed sequences of black discs that were either flashed in one of 37 possible positions on a hexagonal grid (static trials) or smoothly moved through a series of positions on the grid along a straight trajectory (motion trials, Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by Figure 1.

claim: Static trials were presented 252 times per position.
source: Static trials were presented 252 times per position, and each of the 42 motion vectors was presented 108 times.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental design.

claim: Each of the 42 motion vectors was presented 108 times.
source: Static trials were presented 252 times per position, and each of the 42 motion vectors was presented 108 times.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental design.

claim: The stimulus-position likelihood was significantly above chance from 58 ms onward for static stimuli.
source: The stimulus-position likelihood was significantly above chance from 58 ms onward.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2b with statistical testing.

claim: Stimulus positions were decodable from 58 ms after stimulus onset for static stimuli.
source: The stimulus-position likelihood was above chance starting at 58 ms after stimulus onset, meaning that stimulus positions were decodable from this timepoint onward.
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis of decoding performance.

claim: Classifiers trained on the EEG response to static stimuli did not exploit eye movements to determine stimulus position.
source: Therefore, we can conclude that the classifiers trained on the EEG response to the static stimulus did not exploit eye movements to determine the stimulus position.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the analysis showing no significant decoding of stimulus position from eye position data.

claim: For eye position during static trials, stimulus-position likelihood was not significantly above chance at any timepoint.
source: For eye position, stimulus-position likelihood was not significantly above chance at any timepoint, which is in line with previous findings (Blom et al., 2020; Salti et al., 2015; Tse et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of eye tracking data and is consistent with previous research.

claim: The relevant signal for position classification was mainly recorded from occipital electrodes.
source: Finally, Figure 2d shows topographic maps of activation which contributed to classification of stimulus position (Haufe et al., 2014); these show that the relevant signal was mainly recorded from occipital electrodes, suggesting a source within the visual cortex, as expected.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d and is consistent with known visual cortex localization.

claim: The relevant signal for position classification suggests a source within the visual cortex.
source: Finally, Figure 2d shows topographic maps of activation which contributed to classification of stimulus position (Haufe et al., 2014); these show that the relevant signal was mainly recorded from occipital electrodes, suggesting a source within the visual cortex, as expected.
evidence: This inference is based on the topographic distribution of the signal and established neuroanatomy.

claim: Decoding of moving stimulus position was significantly above chance for timepoints between 102 and 180 ms.
source: Permutation testing revealed that decoding was significantly above chance for timepoints between 102 and 180 ms (Figure 3, step 4).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The average stimulus-position likelihood was smaller in magnitude for moving stimuli compared to static stimuli.
source: Although the average stimulus-position likelihood was smaller in magnitude for moving stimuli compared to static stimuli, we observed that the location-specific neural response to motion over time was characterised by a gradual increase of the stimulus-position likelihood as the stimulus approached the centre of the position, then a decrease as the stimulus moved away on the other side.
evidence: This observation is based on the analysis of the time-course of stimulus-position likelihood.

claim: The location-specific neural response to motion was characterized by a gradual increase of stimulus-position likelihood as the stimulus approached the center of the position, then a decrease as it moved away.
source: Although the average stimulus-position likelihood was smaller in magnitude for moving stimuli compared to static stimuli, we observed that the location-specific neural response to motion over time was characterised by a gradual increase of the stimulus-position likelihood as the stimulus approached the centre of the position, then a decrease as the stimulus moved away on the other side.
evidence: This pattern is observed in the data and is similar to findings in cat V1.

claim: The pattern of activity in response to moving stimuli is similar to the pattern found in response to a moving bar in cat V1.
source: This is illustrated in Figure 3, step 5 (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for more training timepoints), and is similar to the pattern of activity found in response to a moving bar with direct recordings from cat V1 (Jancke et al., 2004).
evidence: This comparison is made to previous research in cat V1.

claim: For training timepoints later than approximately 80 ms, Gaussian curves provided a very good fit to the evolution of stimulus-position likelihood over time, with R² values over 0.5.
source: For training timepoints later than ∼80 ms, the Gaussian curves provided a very good fit to the evolution of stimulus-position likelihood over time, with R2 values over 0.5.
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis of the Gaussian fits to the data.

claim: Up to approximately 150 ms training time, the time to peak likelihood increases with increasing training time for moving stimuli.
source: Up to ∼150 ms training time, the time to peak likelihood increases with increasing training time.
evidence: This pattern is observed in Figure 4a.

claim: The sequential pattern of increasing time to peak likelihood with training time is consistent with the first feedforward sweep of stimulus-driven activation.
source: This sequential pattern is consistent with the first feedforward sweep of stimulus-driven activation.
evidence: This interpretation is based on established understanding of visual processing hierarchies.

claim: The order of changes in stimulus representations appeared to be consistent between static and motion trials.
source: The order of these changes appeared to be consistent between static and motion trials.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of the time-courses for static and motion trials.

claim: The pattern of time to peak likelihood reverses between 150 and 200 ms training time.
source: This pattern subsequently reverses between 150 and 200 ms, indicating that hierarchically later representations were activated at a shorter latency.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4a.

claim: From a training time of approximately 250 ms, the time to peak likelihood was stable at approximately 50 ms.
source: Finally, from a training time of ∼250 ms the time to peak likelihood was stable at approximately 50 ms.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4a.

claim: The non-monotonic relationship between training time and time to peak likelihood could reflect feedforward and feedback sweeps of activity in the visual cortex.
source: Perhaps more likely, this pattern could reflect feedforward and feedback sweeps of activity in the visual cortex evoked by the static stimulus: the feedforward sweep activates sequential representations, and information flowing backward along the hierarchy reactivates the same activity patterns in reverse order.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: The timescale of the wave of activity was in line with previous findings showing approximately 10 Hz oscillations evoked by face/house stimuli.
source: The timescale of this wave of activity was in line with previous findings from Dijkstra et al., 2020, who showed approximately 10 Hz oscillations evoked by face/house stimuli.
evidence: This comparison is made to previous research.

claim: Previous TMS, MEG, and fMRI results suggest that 150 ms is a reasonable estimate for the time it takes for visual information to reach hierarchically later visual processing areas such as V5/MT+.
source: Additionally, previous TMS, MEG, and fMRI results suggest that 150 ms is a reasonable estimate for the time it takes for visual information to reach hierarchically later visual processing areas, such as V5/MT+ (Sack et al., 2006; Ahlfors et al., 1999; Hotson et al., 1994; Yoshor et al., 2007; Mohsenzadeh et al., 2018; Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: The first internal knot in the piecewise regression was placed at 158 ms.
source: Corroborating our observation, the first internal knot was placed at 158 ms.
evidence: This is the result of the piecewise regression analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The inflection point at 158 ms was taken as the end of the initial feedforward sweep of information through the visual cortex.
source: We took this inflection point as the end of the initial feedforward sweep of information through the visual cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the piecewise regression analysis.

claim: A linear fit to the static data points relating training time and time to peak likelihood was significantly better than a constant model (F(21,19) = 805.45, p=1.24 × 10⁻¹⁷).
source: A linear fit to the static data points was significantly better than a constant model (F(21,19) = 805.45, p=1.24 × 10–17).
evidence: This is the result of statistical testing of the regression model.

claim: The difference between the static and motion gradients was not significantly different from zero (t=–1.58, p=0.13).
source: Furthermore, the difference between the static and motion gradients was not significantly different from zero (t=–1.58, p=0.13) but the difference between the two intercepts was (t=5.32, p=3.32 × 10–5).
evidence: This is the result of statistical comparison between the two regression lines.

claim: The difference between the static and motion intercepts was significantly different from zero (t=5.32, p=3.32 × 10⁻⁵).
source: Furthermore, the difference between the static and motion gradients was not significantly different from zero (t=–1.58, p=0.13) but the difference between the two intercepts was (t=5.32, p=3.32 × 10–5).
evidence: This is the result of statistical comparison between the two regression lines.

claim: Once position information was available in the cortex, successive cortical representations were sequentially activated along the same time-course for moving and static stimuli.
source: This lack of difference between the gradients means that, once position information was available in the cortex, successive cortical representations were sequentially activated along the same time-course for moving and static stimuli.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the statistical comparison of regression slopes.

claim: Delays that accumulate during cortical processing did not appear to be compensated when processing motion.
source: In other words, delays that accumulate during cortical processing did not appear to be compensated when processing motion.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the lack of difference in regression slopes.

claim: The mean distance between the static and motion regression lines was calculated at 73 ms.
source: The mean distance between the two lines was calculated at 73 ms, implying that the position of a moving object was represented with a latency that was approximately 70 ms shorter than a static object in the same position.
evidence: This is calculated from the regression analysis and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The position of a moving object was represented with a latency that was approximately 70 ms shorter than a static object in the same position.
source: The mean distance between the two lines was calculated at 73 ms, implying that the position of a moving object was represented with a latency that was approximately 70 ms shorter than a static object in the same position.
evidence: This is inferred from the calculated mean distance between regression lines.

claim: For early neural position representations (training times around 70–80 ms), the latency of the peak in the position representation was approximately 0 ms.
source: For early neural position representations (training times around 70–80 ms), the latency of the peak in the position representation was approximately 0ms.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4b where the motion regression line crosses near zero.

claim: Early neural representations were activated at the time that the moving object was physically centered on the corresponding position.
source: In turn, this means that these neural representations were activated at the time that the moving object was physically centred on the corresponding position.
evidence: This is inferred from the approximately 0 ms latency for early representations.

claim: Based on the training time, early stimulus representations likely originated in early visual cortex (V1-3).
source: Based on the training time, these early stimulus representations likely originated in early visual cortex (V1-3), meaning that the early visual system was able to almost completely compensate for neural delays accumulated during processing up to that point and represent moving objects close to their real-time position.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of the representations and established knowledge of visual processing hierarchies.

claim: The early visual system was able to almost completely compensate for neural delays accumulated during processing up to that point and represent moving objects close to their real-time position.
source: Based on the training time, these early stimulus representations likely originated in early visual cortex (V1-3), meaning that the early visual system was able to almost completely compensate for neural delays accumulated during processing up to that point and represent moving objects close to their real-time position.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the data showing near-zero latency for early representations.

claim: This is the first study to demonstrate cross-classification between stationary and smoothly moving stimuli with EEG.
source: This is the first study, to our knowledge, to demonstrate cross-classification between stationary and smoothly moving stimuli with EEG, showing that population neural codes for location are (at least partially) shared between the two stimulus types.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: Population neural codes for location are at least partially shared between stationary and smoothly moving stimuli.
source: This is the first study, to our knowledge, to demonstrate cross-classification between stationary and smoothly moving stimuli with EEG, showing that population neural codes for location are (at least partially) shared between the two stimulus types.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the successful cross-classification between stimulus types.

claim: During the first feedforward sweep of activity, the neural response encoding the position of a moving stimulus was shifted approximately 75 ms earlier than the response to a static stimulus.
source: We subsequently showed that, during the first feedforward sweep of activity, the neural response encoding the position of a moving stimulus was shifted approximately 75 ms earlier than the response to a static stimulus.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of regression lines.

claim: The early decoded representations of the position of a moving stimulus aligned with the real-time position of the object.
source: The early decoded representations of the position of a moving stimulus aligned with the real-time position of the object, rather than the position corresponding to afferent retinal input (subject to transmission and processing delays), which would instead signal outdated position information in visual cortex.
evidence: This is a key finding from the study showing near-zero latency for early representations.

claim: Delay compensation was primarily achieved before information reached visual cortex.
source: Finally, we showed that delay compensation was primarily achieved before information reached visual cortex, as the recorded cortical processing of static and motion stimuli followed a similar time-course.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the similar slopes of the regression lines for static and motion trials.

claim: This study shows direct neural evidence of motion extrapolation enabling accurate real-time representation of moving objects in humans.
source: Overall, this study shows direct neural evidence of motion extrapolation enabling accurate real-time representation of moving objects in humans.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the findings.

claim: Neural recordings from animals and recent fMRI studies in humans have reliably shown RF shifts throughout the visual cortex in response to motion.
source: Neural recordings from animals and more recent fMRI studies in humans have reliably shown RF shifts throughout the visual cortex in response to motion (Harvey and Dumoulin, 2016), and that these displacements are against the direction of motion (Schneider et al., 2019; Sundberg et al., 2006; Fu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: RF shifts in response to motion are against the direction of motion.
source: Neural recordings from animals and more recent fMRI studies in humans have reliably shown RF shifts throughout the visual cortex in response to motion (Harvey and Dumoulin, 2016), and that these displacements are against the direction of motion (Schneider et al., 2019; Sundberg et al., 2006; Fu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Harvey and Dumoulin, 2016, found that RF shifts in response to motion scale with the size of the RF across the visual hierarchy.
source: Harvey and Dumoulin, 2016, found that RF shifts in response to motion scale with the size of the RF across the visual hierarchy.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research.

claim: The results suggest that later visual areas show RF shifts of the same magnitude as earlier visual areas.
source: In contrast, our results suggest that later visual areas show RF shifts of the same magnitude as earlier visual areas.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar slopes of the regression lines.

claim: The early visual response to moving stimuli is shifted in time such that neural delays accumulated up to that point are compensated.
source: We found that the early visual response to moving stimuli is shifted in time, such that the neural delays accumulated up to that point are compensated.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: During subsequent cortical processing, there is no further compensation for delays.
source: However, during subsequent cortical processing, there is no further compensation for delays.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar slopes of the regression lines for static and motion trials.

claim: Retinal ganglion cells respond strongly to the leading edge of moving stimuli.
source: As discussed in the Introduction, retinal ganglion cells respond strongly to the leading edge of moving stimuli (Berry et al., 1999; Johnston and Lagnado, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Responding to the leading edge effectively shifts the encoding of the position of a moving stimulus forward relative to a static stimulus at the earliest stage of processing.
source: This effectively shifts the encoding of the position of a moving stimulus forward relative to a static stimulus at the earliest stage of processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of retinal ganglion cell responses.

claim: Evidence of a latency advantage for moving stimuli has been identified in the cat lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.
source: Additionally, evidence of a latency advantage for moving stimuli has been identified in the cat lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus (Orban et al., 1985), where visual information is transmitted en route to the visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous evidence suggests that pre-cortical mechanisms are not sufficient to account for the extent of compensation for neural delays observed in this study.
source: However, none of the previous evidence suggests that these pre-cortical mechanisms are sufficient to account for compensation for neural delays, to the extent we observe here.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with previous research findings.

claim: Retinal compensation mechanisms only appear to act up to speeds of about 5 degrees visual angle/second (dva/s).
source: In particular, the retinal compensation mechanisms only appear to act up to speeds of about 5 degrees visual angle/second (dva/s) (Berry et al., 1999; Jancke et al., 2004), roughly half the speed used in the current study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is likely that some cortical mechanisms play a role in delay compensation.
source: Therefore, it is likely that some cortical mechanisms play a role.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pre-cortical mechanisms alone are insufficient.

claim: There is evidence that a model of object motion is encoded in MT+ and influences neural response profiles in earlier visual areas through feedback connections.
source: For example, there is evidence that a model of object motion is encoded in MT+, and influences neural response profiles in earlier visual areas through feedback connections (Maus et al., 2013a; Maus et al., 2013b; Nijhawan and Kirschfeld, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Feedback connections could transmit information to neurons into whose RFs the moving stimulus will soon enter, driving an anticipatory response.
source: These feedback connections could transmit information to neurons into whose RFs the moving stimulus will soon enter, driving an anticipatory response.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on previous research.

claim: Within-layer horizontal connections might activate neurons further ahead on the motion path.
source: Similarly, within-layer horizontal connections might activate neurons further ahead on the motion path (Benvenuti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Benvenuti et al., 2020, show that input from feedback and horizontal connections can drive spiking responses in cat V1.
source: Benvenuti et al., 2020, show that this input from feedback and horizontal connections can drive spiking responses in cat V1.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research.

claim: The findings suggest that compensatory mechanisms act only early in the course of stimulus processing and are present only early in the visual cortical hierarchy.
source: Crucially, our findings suggest that these mechanisms act only early in the course of stimulus processing, and therefore are present only early in the visual cortical hierarchy.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the data showing no further compensation during later processing.

claim: Temporal alignment between early representations of the stimulus and its physical position is lost during further processing.
source: Even though we find temporal alignment between the early representations of the stimulus and its physical position, this alignment is lost during further processing.
evidence: This is observed in the data showing accumulation of delays during later processing.

claim: Hogendoorn and Burkitt, 2019, argue that cortical motion extrapolation is necessary to minimize the discrepancy between an internal model of object position and the external world in the case of time-varying stimulation.
source: In a recent theoretical paper, Hogendoorn and Burkitt, 2019, argue that cortical motion extrapolation is necessary to minimise the discrepancy (prediction error) between an internal model of object position and the external world in the case of time-varying stimulation.
evidence: This is a citation to a theoretical paper.

claim: This study suggests that feedforward cortical delays are not compensated.
source: Although the authors claim that the model including feedforward and feedback extrapolation is more parsimonious, this study suggests that feedforward cortical delays are not compensated.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the data showing similar slopes for static and motion trials.

claim: If prediction errors are to be minimized, extrapolation might be implemented only in feedback connections.
source: We therefore support the proposition that, if prediction errors are to be minimised, extrapolation might be implemented only in feedback connections.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings.

claim: Previous EEG research has investigated whether neural delays are compensated when viewing apparent motion.
source: Previous EEG research has investigated whether neural delays are compensated when viewing apparent motion.
evidence: This introduces a comparison to previous research.

claim: Two studies have found evidence of a 15–20 ms latency advantage when processing a stimulus within an apparent motion sequence compared to an unpredictable flash.
source: Although apparent motion is an impoverished motion signal, two studies have found evidence of a 15–20 ms latency advantage when processing a stimulus within an apparent motion sequence compared to an unpredictable flash (Hogendoorn and Burkitt, 2018; Blom et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The latency advantage for apparent motion is substantially less compensation than found in the present study for smooth motion.
source: This is substantially less compensation than we find in the present study, likely due to the lack of continuous stimulation in the case of apparent motion.
evidence: This comparison is made between the current findings and previous research.

claim: An apparent motion stimulus is static on the retina, precluding the gain control mechanism from acting.
source: For example, an apparent motion stimulus is static on the retina, precluding the gain control mechanism described above from acting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of apparent motion stimuli.

claim: Smoothly moving objects trigger a travelling wave of activity that propagates in the visual cortex in front of the retinotopic position of the stimulus.
source: Smoothly moving objects also trigger a travelling wave of activity that propagates in the visual cortex in front of the retinotopic position of the stimulus (Benvenuti et al., 2020), which is different from the non-linear combination of activity elicited by an apparent motion stimulus (Chemla et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The travelling wave of activity for smooth motion is different from the non-linear combination of activity elicited by an apparent motion stimulus.
source: Smoothly moving objects also trigger a travelling wave of activity that propagates in the visual cortex in front of the retinotopic position of the stimulus (Benvenuti et al., 2020), which is different from the non-linear combination of activity elicited by an apparent motion stimulus (Chemla et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Blom et al., 2020, found evidence that a sensory template of an expected apparent motion stimulus is activated before the onset of the stimulus.
source: Blom et al., 2020, additionally found evidence that a sensory template of an expected apparent motion stimulus is activated before the onset of the stimulus, which has additionally been found in monkey V1 (Guo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a citation to previous research.

claim: A limitation of the present study is that the localisation accuracy of moving stimuli was considerably lower than that of static stimuli.
source: A limitation of the present study is that the localisation accuracy of moving stimuli was considerably lower than that of static stimuli.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a limitation by the authors.

claim: Neural populations that encode the position of static stimuli do not completely overlap with neural populations that encode the position of moving objects.
source: This is because classifiers were trained and tested on different stimulus types; neural populations that encode the position of static stimuli do not completely overlap with neural populations that encode the position of moving objects (Noda et al., 1971; Subramaniyan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous fMRI studies show that, following a strong onset response, the neural response to moving stimuli decreases over time.
source: Additionally, previous fMRI studies show that, following a strong onset response, the neural response to moving stimuli decreases over time (Schellekens et al., 2016; Schellekens et al., 2017; Harrison et al., 2007; McKeefry et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The earliest signals containing information about the location of static stimuli were not informative about moving stimuli.
source: We additionally found that the earliest signals containing information about the location of static stimuli were not informative about moving stimuli.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The timing of the earliest flash-evoked activity (approximately 60 ms after stimulus onset) suggests a source within V1.
source: The timing of the earliest flash-evoked activity (∼60 ms after stimulus onset) suggests a source within V1 (Alilović et al., 2019; Fahrenfort et al., 2007; Di Russo et al., 2002; Wibral et al., 2009; Vanni et al., 2004).
evidence: This inference is supported by citations to previous research on V1 response timing.

claim: The position of the moving stimulus was decodable only on the basis of representations formed after approximately 100 ms.
source: In contrast, the position of the moving stimulus was decodable only on the basis of representations formed after approximately 100 ms, suggesting that this analysis approach does not capture the earliest motion-evoked V1 activity.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: There is some evidence that direct connections from either LGN or the pulvinar to MT+ (bypassing V1) are used when processing motion.
source: Alternatively, early processing of motion could be different to static stimuli: there is some evidence that direct connections from either LGN or the pulvinar to MT+ (bypassing V1) are used when processing motion (ffytche et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The flash-lag effect is a visual illusion in which a moving bar is perceived ahead of a flashed bar despite them being physically aligned.
source: Of relevance to these results is the flash-lag effect (FLE), a visual illusion in which a moving bar is perceived ahead of a flashed bar despite them being physically aligned (Nijhawan, 1994).
evidence: This is a description of a well-known visual illusion supported by citation.

claim: The flash-lag effect demonstrates that moving objects are perceived in an extrapolated position.
source: This illusion demonstrates that moving objects are indeed perceived in an extrapolated position.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the flash-lag effect.

claim: The results are congruent only with spatial explanations of the flash-lag effect; temporal models cannot explain how latency shifts could be greater than the latency of the unshifted neural response.
source: However, our results are congruent only with spatial explanations; temporal models cannot explain how latency shifts could be greater than the latency of the unshifted neural response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings in relation to theories of the flash-lag effect.

claim: Parts of the visual system encode moving objects at a position that afferent sensory information could not yet indicate.
source: We show that parts of the visual system encode moving objects at a position that afferent sensory information could not yet indicate.
evidence: This is a key finding from the study showing representations ahead of retinal input.

claim: Early visual areas represent moving objects in their real-time position.
source: We show that, during the first feedforward sweep of activity, the latency of the neural response to moving stimuli is substantially reduced compared to the response to unpredictable static stimuli. The effect of this latency advantage is that early visual areas represent moving objects in their real-time position, suggesting that (potentially a combination of) retinal, subcortical, and cortical extrapolation mechanisms can overcome neural delays very early on in visual processing.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study based on the data analysis.

claim: Retinal, subcortical, and cortical extrapolation mechanisms can overcome neural delays very early on in visual processing.
source: The effect of this latency advantage is that early visual areas represent moving objects in their real-time position, suggesting that (potentially a combination of) retinal, subcortical, and cortical extrapolation mechanisms can overcome neural delays very early on in visual processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings showing early compensation for delays.

claim: Additional delays accumulated during subsequent cortical processing appear not to be compensated.
source: Additional delays accumulated during subsequent cortical processing appear not to be compensated.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the similar slopes of regression lines for static and motion trials.

claim: The visual system predictively encodes the position of moving stimuli.
source: These results demonstrate that the visual system predictively encodes the position of moving stimuli, and provide an evidence base to constrain models of how and when motion extrapolation is achieved in the human visual system.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all findings.

claim: Twelve participants completed all six testing sessions and were included in analyses.
source: Twelve participants (two male; mean age = 27.0 years, s.d.=4.93 years) completed all six testing sessions and were included in analyses.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the study sample.

claim: Stimuli were black, filled circles with a radius of 1.29 dva presented in a hexagonal configuration with 37 possible stimulus positions.
source: Stimuli were black, filled circles with a radius of 1.29 dva presented in a hexagonal configuration with 37 possible stimulus positions.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the stimulus design.

claim: The stimulus moved at a velocity of 10.36 dva/s in motion trials.
source: A trial consisted of the stimulus flashing in a single location on the grid for 250 ms (static trials), or moving in a straight line at a velocity of 10.36 dva/s through the grid (motion trials), such that the amount of time spent travelling the length of the stimulus diameter was the same as the duration of the static stimulus.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the stimulus motion.

claim: It took 400 ms for the stimulus to travel between grid positions in motion trials.
source: The stimulus passed through between four and seven flash positions, depending on the eccentricity of the vector, taking 400 ms to travel between grid positions.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the stimulus timing.

claim: Continuous EEG data were recorded at 2048 Hz using a 64-channel BioSemi Active-Two system.
source: Continuous EEG data were recorded at 2048 Hz using a 64-channel BioSemi Active-Two system (BioSemi, Amsterdam, The Netherlands), connected to a standard 64-electrode EEG cap.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data acquisition.

claim: EEG data were down-sampled to 128 Hz to reduce computation time and memory load.
source: Data were down-sampled to 128 Hz to reduce computation time and memory load required for further pre-processing and analysis.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data preprocessing.

claim: No filtering was applied to data so as not to distort event timing.
source: No filtering was applied to data so as not to distort event timing (van Driel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citation.

claim: Linear discriminant analysis classifiers with a shrinkage regularisation parameter of 0.05 were trained to discriminate the location of static stimuli.
source: Linear discriminant analysis classifiers with a shrinkage regularisation parameter of 0.05 (Mostert et al., 2015) were trained to discriminate the location of static stimuli and tested on unseen static trials or motion trials.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the classification analysis.

claim: Classifiers were trained using pairwise combinations of stimulus positions.
source: To avoid bias that often emerges from multi-class classification (Yan et al., 2021), classifiers were trained using pairwise combinations of stimulus positions, such that a classifier was trained to discriminate each location from every other location.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the classification approach.

claim: This resulted in 666 trained classifiers at 90 timepoints over a 350 ms period.
source: As it is redundant to train classifiers to discriminate for example, position 1 vs. 2 and also 2 vs. 1, this resulted in 666 trained classifiers at 90 timepoints over a 350 ms period (from stimulus onset at 0 to 100 ms after stimulus offset).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the number of classifiers.
